meta.purpose: Reusable pieces and templates for a Japanese sentence-building game.
meta.romanization: Keeps the same romaji style as cards.json (kyou, doujou, renshuu, etc.).
notes: Vocabulary is grouped by category to avoid repeating type on every entry.
Verb forms are polite forms because the learner prioritizes -masu/-desu speech.
Japanese verb tense is modeled as nonpast/past. Future time words use nonpast forms.
Fixed expressions that are not useful for recombination are listed under excluded.
Templates reference reusable vocab items (including via fixed slots) and keep only grammatical glue in literals; meaningful words are always shown as cards.

verbs.notes: Kept available, but generic generation is limited because quoted/content clauses are not modeled yet.

tense: Each time item exposes allowed timeRef values.
kinou and ototoi allow only past; ashita and asatte allow only nonpast.
kyou, recurring expressions and neutral periods may allow both past and nonpast when context permits.
Japanese future uses the nonpast form: ashita + ikimasu, not a separate future conjugation.
If no time is selected, default to nonpast unless the round explicitly chooses past.
polarity: Choose affirmative or negative independently of tense only when the template allows it.
The selected verb form must match both tense and polarity.
particles: Use each verb argument's particle; do not guess particles from category alone.
Action location normally uses de; destination uses ni; companion uses to; direct object uses o.
Possession uses no; topic constructions use wa; suki and wakarimasu commonly use ga.
adjectives: Predicative polite form: noun wa adjective desu for both i- and na-adjectives.
Before a noun: i-adjectives attach directly; na-adjectives require na.
When a template combines a noun/category with an adjective, only use adjectives whose accepts list contains that noun category.
Category constraints should prevent clearly nonsensical combinations such as oishii + jacket or shizuka + curry.
generation: A template chooses a compatible verb first, then fills only slots accepted by that verb.
Optional slots may be omitted; never fill every slot just because it exists.
The game may create semantically odd but grammatically valid sentences; category constraints should prevent obviously invalid pairings such as eating a jacket.
subjects: When a person slot is the grammatical subject of a verbal sentence, use wa by default.
Example: Hana + sushi + tabemasu -> Hana wa sushi o tabemasu.
Do not add wa when the person is used as a companion (to) or possessor (no).

audit.important: Counts are not expected to equal sourceCards: one source sentence can yield several reusable pieces, while duplicate/contextual cards collapse into one piece.

categorySchema.time: time expressions; timeRef controls verb tense when possible
categorySchema.place: locations/destinations; tags distinguish actionLocation, origin, country, city
categorySchema.person: people/roles that can be subjects, companions or possessors
categorySchema.object: general physical nouns; optional tags refine compatibility
categorySchema.sport: sports accepted by shimasu and often renshuu shimasu
categorySchema.adjective: descriptive predicates; adjClass supports noun modification
categorySchema.state: ready-made state predicates not treated as simple adjectives
categorySchema.question: interrogatives
categorySchema.predicate: relational predicates (e.g. gustar, ser originario de) referenced only via fixed template slots
categorySchema.marker: sentence-type markers (e.g. question) shown as their own card, not text glue

resolver.categoryTag: media:readable -> entries in vocab.media whose tags include readable
resolver.verbArg: verb.args.object -> categories/tags accepted by the selected verb's object argument
